questions.q: Define the difference between "setting" and "atmosphere" in a literary text. Give one example of each from the opening paragraph of "The Tiger King."
questions.a: Setting is the where/when/who-context (Pratibandapuram, colonial era, royal court); atmosphere is the mood created (fable-like, mythic, slightly absurd). In the opening, the setting detail "Maharaja of Pratibandapuram... His Highness Jamedar-General..." establishes a feudal Indian princely state; the atmosphere is created by "Even the threat of a Stuka bomber will not throw me off track" — a jarring anachronism (WWII bomber in a maharaja tale) that signals satirical, tongue-in-cheek tone. A wrong answer that conflates the two (e.g., "setting is the mood") reveals the student cannot separate physical context from emotional effect.

questions.q: The story opens with a ten-day-old infant speaking in complete sentences and questioning astrologers. Explain how this detail establishes the story's atmosphere, and why a realistic setting would undermine Kalki's satirical purpose.
questions.a: The speaking infant immediately signals a fable/folktale atmosphere — we are in a world where logic is suspended, exaggeration is normal, and the supernatural is mundane. This prepares the reader for a satire where a grown Maharaja's obsession with killing 100 tigers is treated with the same matter-of-fact tone. If the setting were realistic (a normal baby, rational astrologers), the Maharaja's later actions would read as madness or tragedy, not satire. The fable atmosphere lets Kalki mock power without demanding psychological realism. A wrong answer focusing only on "magic realism" misses the satirical function: the atmosphere is a frame that makes the absurdity readable as critique.

questions.q: In Section III, the Maharaja bans tiger hunting by anyone except himself and threatens confiscation of property for "fling[ing] so much as a stone at a tiger." Identify the setting details (physical, social, historical) in this passage and explain how they create a bureaucratic-absurdist atmosphere.
questions.a: Physical: "innumerable forests in the Pratibandapuram State" — a ruler's domain. Social: proclamation issued, penalties enforced — feudal law. Historical: "State banned tiger hunting" — princely state autonomy under British paramountcy. These details create a bureaucratic-absurdist atmosphere because the language mimics official government orders ("proclamation was issued," "wealth and property would be confiscated") applied to a personal, obsessive quest. The contrast between formal administrative tone and the Maharaja's private vow ("attend to all other matters only after killing the hundred tigers") generates satire. A wrong answer listing only "forest" or "palace" misses how social/historical setting (feudal proclamation) interacts with character motive to produce atmosphere.

questions.q: Compare the atmosphere of the forest hunting scenes (Sections III–IV) with the toy shop scene (Section V). How does the shift in physical setting — from vast forests to a cramped toyshop — mirror the shift in the Maharaja's fate?
questions.a: Forest scenes: expansive, dangerous, the Maharaja dominates ("Each time it was the Maharaja who won"), atmosphere tense but controlled — he commands the space. Toy shop: confined, domestic, trivial ("wooden tiger cost only two annas and a quarter"), atmosphere mundane then grotesque — a sliver from a cheap toy kills him. The shift from open wilderness where he performs power to a closed commercial space where he is a mere customer mirrors his journey from absolute ruler to mortal victim of chance. The forest allowed him to stage his defiance of prophecy; the toyshop delivers the prophecy's fulfillment through absurd irony. A wrong answer describing only "forest = scary, shop = safe" misses the structural parallel: both settings are stages where the Maharaja's agency is tested and ultimately nullified.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the hillside village setting (Section V: "sheep began to disappear frequently from a hillside village") in advancing the plot AND sustaining the satirical atmosphere. Is this setting merely functional, or does it deepen the critique?
questions.a: The village setting is both functional (provides the hundredth tiger) and satirically rich. Functionally, it supplies the tiger when forests are empty. Satirically, it exposes the Maharaja's tyranny: he announces "three-year exemption from all taxes" — a feudal lord buying loyalty — and when the tiger hides, "Many officers lost their jobs," showing how his obsession destabilizes governance. The villagers' fear ("ran to inform the Maharaja") contrasts with the dewan's later covert operation (smuggling a zoo tiger). The setting deepens the critique by showing how a ruler's personal vanity disrupts ordinary lives and corrupts administration. A wrong answer calling it "just a plot device" ignores how setting in satire extends the target from individual to system.

questions.q: Write a 100-word paragraph establishing a satirical atmosphere for a modern political leader obsessed with a trivial personal record (e.g., most selfies taken, longest speech). Use setting details (office, staff, media, public spaces) to create the mood without naming the satire directly.
questions.a: A strong answer uses bureaucratic language for absurd acts: "The Secretariat issued Circular 447-B: all junior officers to report at 0400 hrs for the Daily Selfie Audit. The corridor outside the Chief Minister's office smelled of floor polish and anxiety. Three photographers on rotation. A dedicated server farm hummed in the basement, storing 14.2 million images. The opposition leader's press conference was rescheduled — again — because the backdrop lighting clashed with the CM's preferred filter. A villager's petition on water scarcity lay unopened on the desk, its paper yellowing beside the ring light." This mirrors Kalki: official tone, trivial obsession, neglected duty, physical details (smell, light, paper) creating atmosphere. A weak answer states the satire explicitly ("It was funny how...") instead of letting setting convey it.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Setting refers to the time, place, and social-historical context in which a story unfolds; atmosphere is the emotional mood or feeling evoked in the reader through ______ details of the setting, sensory imagery, and narrative tone.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're watching a period drama where the palace glitter hides ______ — that's the world Kalki builds.
What is Setting? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Setting refers to the time, place, and social-historical context in which a story unfolds; atmosphere is the emotional mood or feeling evoked in the reader through descriptive details of the setting, sensory imagery, and narrative tone.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify at least three distinct setting layers (physical, historical, social) in "The Tiger King," cite specific textual details for each, and explain how Kalki uses these details to create a satirical atmosphere that shifts from fable-like to tense to darkly ironic across the narrative.
